ORIGINAL PAPER
Anaerobic Co‑digestion Mill Wastewater—Activated Sludge Effect 
of Aerobic Pretreatment on the Performance of OMW Anaerobic 
Digestion
Khalideh Al bkoor Alrawashdeh1   · Abdullah H. Al‑Essa1
Received: 1 October 2018 / Accepted: 6 August 2019 / Published online: 4 September 2019 
© Springer Nature B.V. 2019
Abstract
Aerobic treatment of olive mill wastewater (OMW) is a promising technique for biogas recovery using anaerobic digestion, 
in the case of OMW it is possible to reduce polyphenols and TCOD concentration which undesirable by microorganism 
metabolism. OMW was subjected to the aeration process over different periods to detect the removal efficiency of polyphenols 
and TCOD. During this study, anaerobic co-digestion of OMW without pretreatment and activated sludge (AS) was inhibited 
due to the presence of a high inhibitors concentration. While anaerobic co-digestion of aerated OMW–AS were achieved 
TCOD removal 56.34%, 70.32%, 52.81% and polyphenols removal 42.69%, 60.45%, 63.51% when the OMW aerated for 
2, 4 and 6 days respectively. The highest biogas production 0.473 ­Nm3/kg VS was achieved by OMW aerated for 4 days in 
conjunction with 68.39% CH4, 55.85% VS removal, 10.91 g/l of TCOD and 4.23 g ­CaCO3/l.

Statement of Novelty
This study provides new data about the potential of pre-
treatment of olive mill wastewater co-digestion with 
activated sludge. Pretreatment conducted by the aerobic 
process and detected the best period to applied aerobic 
process to achieve higher COD and polyphenols reduc-
tion. This technique maximized the biogas production con-
junction with high VS, TCOD and polyphenols removal 
efficiency.
Introduction
Among the possible renewable energy sources, biowaste 
from activated sludge (AS) is a promising resource [1]. 
An attractive process solution for cancelling accumulation 
of active sludge is the anaerobic digestion (AD) process 
[2–5]. Therefore, AD of the AS with higher volatile solids 
(VS) content has been considered to be an alternative to 
biomass digestion without competition to food production 
[6, 7].
Thus, VS content higher than 4% in comparison to the 
conventional AD processes from other sources which have 
TS 0.5–3%, could operate by using existing AD infrastruc-
ture at wastewater plants [2–4]. Moreover, the short resi-
dence time for complete digestion of AS from 16–46 days 
were reported when total solid (TS) with removal rate 32% 
of VS increased from 1.79 to 15.67% [8].
The AD inhibitors AS were believed to be directly 
related to the decreased capacity of functional microor-
ganisms. Microbial communities may also differ due to 
the accumulation of volatile Fatty Acids (VFA) combined 
with high, thus leads to alternation in metabolic pathways 
and decrease AD performance. On the other hand, various 
suggestions were presented to avoid inhibition through co-
digestion technology [3, 6, 7, 9, 10]. In practical, using AD 
to co-digest AS with other biowaste materials to improve 
biogas production has been proposed and implemented at 
the wastewater plant [2–5], that can be achieved by using 
existing infrastructure at the wastewater plant without 
extra capital cost.
The world production of olive oil in 2017 about 2.945 
million tons and according to provisional figures by the 
International Olive Council (IOC), the Global olive oil 
production is increased to rise by 28% for 2018. The by-
products of Olive oil mills such as olive mill wastewaters 
(OMW), could be considered as suitable feedstock for the 
AD process. Actually, those by-products of Olive oil mills 
pose a serious risk, where the organic compounds meas-
ured as 40 g/l to 220 g/l [11, 12]. However, OMW was 
subjected to many treatment studies in terms of physical 
and chemical treatment [13–17], one of the satisfactory 
solutions to dispose of these organic pollutants is the AD 
process [18, 19].
However, the AD of OMW suffered low pH value, high 
content of phenolic, and ammonium nitrogen lack, which 
lead to inhibition. Currently, to overcome these limitations, 
pretreatments for OMW have been reported such as aerobic 
process and evaporation in storage ponds. In order to encour-
age bacterial growth, aeration as a pretreatment process had 
been applied with different technologies. That approves 
digestion process efficiency and high polyphenols rates [20]. 
The Polyphenol molecular structure is concerned as one 
of the main toxicity reasons. When the Hydroxyl Number 
Group (HNG) decreases the inhibitory effect is increased, 
HNG is associated with polyphenols concentration [21].
Many studies showed that OMW could be improved with 
low dilution by drying without adding chemical substances, 
also could be subject to co-digestion process with AS which 
contains a high level of ammonium nitrogen. Co-digestion of 
AS with OMW provides the necessary nutrients and buffer 
capacity also decrease potential inhibitors of the AD process 
[16–22].
The biogas production and methane content are based 
on an improved composition of the substrate to be ready 
for AD, since each one of the substrates complements other 
deficiency. Biogas production is significantly increased 
when co-substrate is used [23–28].
This work study reports on the use of the pretreatment 
technique of OMW by aerobic digestion. Also, presents an 
investigation of the pretreated OMW effect on the perfor-
mance of codigestion process with AS, biogas and methane 
production. Previous tests of aerobic before AD process 
were performed to determine the suitable time of aeration 
to achieve maximum COD and polyphenols reduction. Aer-
ated OMW with ratio 50% volume/volume to AS were car-
ried out by the Biomethane Potential (BMP). This technique 
was implemented by other authors through AD and aerobic 
processes, achieving high efficiency of the digestion process 
in terms of biogas production and eliminating organic load 
[16, 17, 29].
Methodology—Materials and Methods
Feedstock
OMW was extracted from a two-phase oil extraction that 
belongs to the olive harvest seasons of 2017. OMW was 
collected in 20 l Jerrycan. AS was obtained from secondary 
sludge of a wastewater treatment plant WWTP of Irbid city 
(Actual load in the range of 8635.1–9000 ­m3/d and 8276.9 
­m3/d of hydraulic load outside), Jordan. OMW and AS were

stored at 4 °C until use. According to UNI 5667-13/2000, 
all the samples used in the BMP tests were prepared. Co-
substrates of pretreated and non-treated OMW and AS were 
homogenized using a manual shaking (2 times /day for 1 min) 
and were prepared on a volume (v/v) basis. Raw materials 
were analyzed of both physico-chemical characteristics and 
proximate analysis through TGA [30]. The characteristics 
include the humidity U, total solid TS, viscosity solid VS, ASH 
and fixed Carbon F.C, thus analysis was optioned according 
to the standard methods as described Alrawashdeh et al. [5]. 
The raw material characteristics are summarized in Table 1.
Experimental Setup
A manual batch aerobic reactor was prepared which consists 
of a vessel of 3 l realized in Broro-silicate glass and has the 
injection of air is fixed at the bottom of the vessel using an air 
compressor in which the flow rate of air is 0.5 l/l substrate/
min. The temperature of the substrate was room atmosphere 
(25–28 °C).
The BMP tests were prepared in closed vessels of 1 l (Boro-
silicate glass) which are conducted with two necks, one to 
extract and introduce the feedstock, and the other to collect the 
generated biogas during the process. Vessels were reproduc-
ibility of the tests in order to reliable results.
The biogas volume generated during the experiment is 
measured using the biogas measurement method as described 
in [31]. The generated biogas was investigated and analyzed by 
GC as described Alrawashdeh et al. [5]. The vessels operated 
in semi conditions under mesophilic conditions (35 ± 2 °C) 
using water bath surrounding vessels. The vessel content of 
which was homogenized using manual shaking, allowing for 
complete mixing. In order to avoid conditions of pressurized, 
the generated biogas in excess was vented through extraction 
neck using siring.
Experimental Procedure
A set of aerobic tests were carried out to investigate the time of 
aeration that achieves maximum reduction of COD and poly-
phenols of the OMW substrates. Afterwards, AD tests were 
performed using pretreated and non-treated OMW as co-sub-
strate with AS substrate without adding any inoculum, given 
that anaerobic bacteria already present in the AS substrate.
The samples of OMW substrate were prepared in sepa-
rated experiment tests, i.e., one test from 2 to 10 days. In 
each test, the aerobic reactor was filled up to 1 l (50% of 
reactor volume). Before the AD test all, the pretreated OMW 
substrates were sorted at 4 °C.
To identify the effects of the aerobic process as a pre-
treatment technique to achieve higher anaerobic digestion 
efficiency, a set of parameter measurements was performed 
during the process. Thus parameters, including TCOD, TS 
and polyphenols reduction and pH value “hydrogen ion con-
centration”. The samples of pretreated OMW were analyzed 
to identify the best period of aeration.
Next, all the AD vessels were filled up to 20% of their 
volume (200 ml) with different co-substrate of OMW-AS 
prepared as recommended in similar studies [5]. A set of 
the mixture was utilized 50% v/v of AS -pretreated OMW 
(for different periods 2–10 days), in addition, 50% v/v of 
AS–OMW (non-treated), in order to investigate the aeration 
effects on biogas production and TCOD reduction.
The AD tests were operating in semi-continuous mode, 
the volume of OMW was added daily into the vessel and 
the same quantity was extracted from the vessel, therefore 
the flow rate of 10 ml of OMW/ day. The tests were per-
formed for 40 days, biogas, methane and degradation level 
were obtained. The maximum degradation and Hydraulic 
Residence Time (HRT) are defined based on the time that 
bacterial metabolism takes place. The 1st HRT was the adap-
tation period of in which the VS concentration was increased 
due to co-substrate replaced by OMW during introduce 
and extraction substrate. While the 2nd HRT was stability 
period that presents the steady state degradation, therefore 
the effluent analysis was showed decreases of TCOD reduc-
tion, biogas production was stabilized and the pH values 
were constant.
Produced Biogas was investigated using water replace-
ment method [31], the compositions of biogas were analyzed 
and detected for each test. Both samples of influent and efflu-
ent were analyzed to detect the U, TS, VS, ASH and F.C, in 
addition, the values TCOD reduction and pH. Table 2 shows 
the characteristics and parameters of the operating of pre-
treated OMW and co-substrate which fed to AD tests. Proxi-
mate analysis was performed using Thermographic Analysis 
(TGA), the TCOD was detected using Nano colour kits and 
spectrophotometer (Macherey–Nagel).
Produced biogas was sampled using gas-tight syringes 
(250 μl) and collected via rubber stopper of the small neck 
of the vessel. Samples of biogas were analyzed in duplicate 
by a gas chromatograph (490 micro GC, Agilent Technolo-
gies, SC, CA, USA. GC was used to detect the quantity of 
the ­(CH4, ­CO2, CO, ­C2, ­O2 and ­N2). GC consists of a thermal

Results and Discussion
The main parameter measurements during the aerobic pro-
cess were obtained as shown in Figs. 1 and 2. By tracing the 
graph it can be observed that the effect of increasing aeration 
period was reflected on the TCOD reduction, polyphenols 
concentration and VS reduction. There was a decreasing 
trend in the concentration of polyphenols. In the fourth day 
it was reduced to 4.1 g/kg TS, but the reduction after 6 days 
it remained in the range of 0.1–0.2 g/kg TS and the down-
ward trend continued over the following days.
An intense increase in the TCOD reduction was also 
noticed during the process, where the range of reduction was 
1–17% from the 1st to the 10th day of the aeration period, 
and the greatest reduction of the TCOD was observed from 
the 1st day to 4th day with 12%. As shown Fig. 2 the con-
centration of TCOD, polyphenols and VS were measured as 
the function of TS, A slight decreasing in VS concentration 
was noticed and after the 4th day, there was a small portion 
of decrement as a result of the stability of aeration process. 
It should be noted that during aerobic degradation there were 
decreasing in TS as a result of evaporation in conjunction 
with aerobic degradation.
Give the polyphenols results the maximum reduction 50% 
was achieved in 4 days and from 4th day to the 6th day was 
achieved 1% while from 6th day to 8th day only 10%. So, 
increase the time of aeration after the 4 days was not feasible 
in term of polyphenols reduction. The same results were 
noticed in the case of TCOD, where the TCOD reduction 
can be described as a stable period compared to pre-day 4.
Investigating the results, it can be shown that the maxi-
mum reduction rate of polyphenols was found to be around 
50%. This reduction was achieved in the first 4 days. From 
the 4th to 6th day and from 6th to 8th days, a reduction of 
11% was achieved, whereas a reduction of 10% was achieved 
from the 8th to 10th days (in total 70% for 10 of aeration). 
From these results, it can be shown that the reduction poly-
phenols verse the aeration time isn’t directly proportional 
and the cutoff period, for best reduction results is 4 days.
Over the aeration time, an increase in the pH value of 
the OMW substance was observed from 4.4 to 5.2 without 
modifying their pH value. The maximum pH value was 
achieved in the 4th day, also C/N ratio was detected dur-
ing the process which its value was in the range of 22 to 
36. Similar studies were conducted to detect the effect of

aerobic treatment of olive mill wastewater, thus confirmed 
with our result in this study. El Hajjouji et al. [29] reported 
that aeration treatment of OMW could increase the effi-
ciency of polyphenols reduction, where the maximum 
reduction was achieved about 94% in junction with pH 
about 5.99 and 5.99 of C/N. Essays made by Gonzalez and 
Cuadros [16] showed that the pretreatment was used with 
providing air in the flow rate of 0.65 l/l reactor, this study 
achieved maximum polyphenols degradation for 7 days, 
which were the same trend in our treatment for 4 days. In 
another study Michailides et al. [20], the researchers used 
aeration of OMW with continuous recirculation under one 
day of HRT, this technique reduced 50% of the concentra-
tion of phenolic, according to them increase the aeration 
time does not achieve a higher reduction in polyphenols 
concentration.
Given the results of pretreatment tests of OMW, four 
anaerobic digestion tests (with duplicates to investigate the 
accuracy of the result) were prepared using co-substrate 
of OMW and AS. One vessel filled up to 20% of its vol-
ume with 50% of non-treated OMW and 50% AS, other 
vessels filled with the same configuration, but instead, 
non-treated OMW in each test used pretreated OMW for 
2 days, 4 days and 6 days. However, the tests didn’t include 
pretreated OMW sample because as mentioned before, 
after the 6 days of aeration time it had reached stability in 
the case of TCOD degradation and lowest reduction in the 
case of polyphenols. Table 3 shows the characteristics and 
the configuration of co-substrate were used in anaerobic 
digestion.
The anaerobic tests were conducted for 40 days with 
25 days of HRT, where the organic loading ORL flow rate 
was 10 ml OMW/ day for all tests, ORL of OMW was the 
same as a configuration of the OMW used in each test.
The biogas yields of all tests shown in Fig. 3, where 
the biogas production considered as a function of TCOD 
removed from the co-substrate. Overall, the anaerobic co-
digestion process, the first 25 days were the acclimation 
period, then reached steady state for the co-digestion of 
pretreated OMW and AS. While co-digestion of untreated 
OMW–AS was suffered from inhibition after 15 days as a 
result of high polyphenols and TCOD concentration and 
low value of pH. It should be indicating that even if OMW 
is added to AS (rich in anaerobic bacteria and has high pH 
value), the digestion unviable.
Co-digestion of OMW aerated for 2 days showed low 
biogas production at the initial period then after 20 days 
was inhibited due to buffer accumulation as a result of 
organic load and polyphenols concentration. Similarly, 
as illustrated in Fig. 3, co-digestion of OMW aerated for 
6 days was trended to produce biogas at a high rate during 
HRT period then dramatically decreased. While co-diges-
tion of OMW aerated for 4 days showed the highest biogas 
yield that related to a lower concentration of polyphenols 
and TCOD and high pH value.
Tables 3 and 4 specify the results and characteristic 
of co-substrate and digested, as illustrated high dissolved 
efficiencies of TCOD removal (70.33%) achieved by co-
digestion of OMW aerated for 4 days and AS, while the 
non-aerated OMW achieved the lowest efficiency of TCOD 
removal.
Table 3 illustrates the monitoring pH value for all 
digested. During the untreated OMW–AS test period, 
the pH was not stable 4.9–6.1 in which unfavourable 
for bacterial, while during aerated OMW and AS diges-
tion pH was approximately stable. Figure 4 shows the

concentration of TCOD during the anaerobic co-digestion 
of WAS-AS which reflects the effect of aerobic digestion 
as pretreatment.
VS reduction was used as assessing the performance 
of the anaerobic digestion process, during the process VS 
degraded then converted to biogas. Among co-digestion 
OMW aerated for 4 days and AS showed the highest VS 
reduction 0f 55%, which agrees with 70.32% of TCOD 
removal and 60.45 of polyphenols removal. Also, this 
result showed that as the organic load increased, it presents 
the lowest biogas production and the lowest capability of 
degradation.
However, the result of anaerobic tests showed that co-
digestion with untreated OMW lead to inhibit and even 
destabilize the process of anaerobic, this inhibition asso-
ciated with polyphenols which lead to the toxicity of sub-
strate which clearly appeared in the performance of diges-
tion process. For this reason OMW substrate is required, 
that agrees with El-Hajjouji et al. [29]; Olivier et al. [10]; 
Belaid et al. [32]; Oz and Uzun [33] and Alrawashdeh 
[31].
Conclusion
Olive mill wastewater has a high concentration of polyphe-
nols and Alkalinity balance lack; thus aerobic treatment of 
OMW could be a promising perspective on anaerobic diges-
tion AD. This technique can achieve the highest removal of 
pollutants. The result of AD showed that the highest poly-
phenols removal efficiency 60.45% was achieved by OMW 
aerated for 4 days, where the results show, as increase the 
aeration time, the polyphenols reduction increasing.
Also, the results show that the optimum aeration period is 
4 days for anaerobic digestion process, which it was achieved 
the highest biogas production 0.44 ­Nm3/kg VS with quality 
68.39% of CH4 in the conjunction of 55.82% and TCOD 
removal 70.32%.
The biogas production of untreated OMW with AS was 
inhibited (0.132 ­Nm3/kgCOD, 8.1 ­gCaCO3/l of Alkalinity con-
centration and 36.03 g/l of TCOD) due to high polyphenols 
and pollutants continent and low pH value which were led to 
the lowest VS degradation. Using co-digestion of pretreated 
OMW and AS improve the pH value, C/N ratio, an organic 
load required from methanogenic bacteria. However, the 
organic loading rate of pretreated OMW should be low in 
order to avoid conditions of overloading and buffer accumu-
lation which leads to inhibit the AD process.
